note: 打球 dǎ qiú 'to play ball' (basketball, baseball and similar); 踢球 tī qiú 'to play soccer'.
Usually said with 了: 我忘了 'I forgot'. Means the same as 忘記 wàng jì. The literary reading wáng is not used in speech.

example.english: I forgot to bring my keys.

note: Any line, string, cable or route (an MRT or bus line). The measure word is 條 tiáo.

example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo xiàn tài duǎn le.

note: Usually followed by 都 dōu: 每天都… 'every day (without fail)…'.

hint: rice and dishes in a box
note: A Taiwan staple: rice with a main dish and sides, bought for lunch or dinner (排骨便當 pái gǔ biàn dāng 'pork chop bento'). The word comes from Japanese bentō. MOE also lists biàn dang with a light second syllable. 便 is biàn here, not pián as in 便宜.

example.english: I'm having a bento for lunch.

note: Counts sets such as glasses (一副眼鏡), gloves and decks of cards, and facial expressions (一副很累的樣子 'looking all tired'). As a prefix it means 'vice- / deputy': 副總統 'vice president'. A rare literary reading is pì.

example.pinyin: Wǒ xūyào yī fù xīn yǎnjìng.
example.english: I need a new pair of glasses.

gloss: to make use of; to exploit
note: It can be neutral ('make good use of time') or negative ('use / exploit a person'). For plain 'to use' a tool, say 用.

example.english: You should make good use of your time.

note: A casual and slightly cheeky way to refer to a person: 這傢伙 'this guy'. It can sound rude about a stranger.
Both the verb and the noun: 設計師 shè jì shī 'designer'.

example.trad: 這件衣服的設計很特別。
example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu de shèjì hěn tèbié.
example.english: This outfit has a really unusual design.

note: Insist on something (堅持要… 'insist on…') or keep going without giving up (再堅持一下 'hang in there a bit longer').

hint: with a finger, like a button
note: Press with a finger: buttons, doorbells, keys. Pushing a door or person is 推 tuī. In formal speech 按照 means 'according to'.
Polyphone: dāi 'to stay (somewhere)'; dài in 等待 'to wait', 對待 'to treat (someone)' and 待遇 'pay, treatment'. Compare 住 zhù 'to live somewhere'.

example.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒ xiǎng dāi zài jiālǐ.
example.english: This weekend I want to stay home.

gloss: to be affected by; to receive
note: Means you undergo or experience something, usually followed by an abstract noun: 受到影響 'be affected', 受到歡迎 'be welcomed', 受到批評 'be criticized'. Don't confuse it with 收到 shōu dào 'to receive (a package or message)'.

example.pinyin: Nǐ bùyào zhème kuài jiù fàngqì.

note: Taiwan usually says 早餐 (the mainland often says 早飯). The 早餐店 zǎo cān diàn 'breakfast shop' is a Taiwan institution. Lunch is 午餐 wǔ cān or 午飯 wǔ fàn.
'Late' in time (太晚了 'it's too late', 晚一點 'a bit later'), and 'evening' in words like 今晚 and 晚安 'good night'. The usual word for 'evening' is 晚上.

example.pinyin: Tài wǎn le, kuài qù shuìjiào.
example.english: It's too late, go to bed.

note: 好麻煩 'what a hassle'. 麻煩你… 'could you please…' is a very common polite request. MOE gives a neutral tone, má fan, but many Taiwanese say má fán.

example.english: Could you please open the door for me?

hint: all the way until, two syllables
note: Often paired with 才 cái: 直到昨天才… 'not until yesterday did…'. Don't confuse it with 知道 zhī dào 'to know', which differs only in the first tone.

example.pinyin: Tā zhídào zuótiān cái gàosu wǒ.
example.english: He didn't tell me until yesterday.

note: Taiwan standard (MOE) reading is tú rán; the mainland says tū rán. Both are understood.
Same meaning as 很多 hěn duō, which is far more common in casual speech.

example.english: There are a lot of people in the park.

note: In everyday Taiwan speech it is often 嘴巴 zuǐ ba. 嘴很甜 'sweet-talking', 閉嘴 bì zuǐ 'shut up'. 口 kǒu is 'mouth' mainly in compounds and as 'opening, entrance'.
Hurting someone physically or emotionally; also a noun, 'harm, damage'. Getting injured yourself is 受傷 shòu shāng.

example.english: I don't want to hurt you.

note: Taiwan (MOE) reads both syllables with full tones, yǎn jīng; the mainland makes the second one neutral (yǎn jing).
Go back somewhere else, away from the speaker; 回來 means 'come back here'. MOE gives a neutral tone, but Taiwanese often say huí qù, especially when it ends the sentence.
Also 晚飯 wǎn fàn. 吃晚餐 chī wǎn cān 'to have dinner'.
The somewhat formal noun. In casual talk people say 錯 cuò: 是我的錯 'it's my fault'.

example.pinyin: Zhè fèn bàogào yǒu hěn duō cuòwù.
example.english: This report has a lot of mistakes.

note: The MOE standard form is written 祕密, but 秘密 is very common in Taiwan. The pronunciation is the same.
After a time or number it means 'and a half': 三點半 'half past three', 一個半 'one and a half'. 一半 yī bàn means 'half (of it)'.
不 'not' + 再 'again'; it often ends with 了. Spoken bú zài (不 changes to a 2nd tone before a 4th tone).

example.pinyin: Tā bù zài shì xiǎoháizi le.

note: Deeper meaning or value: 很有意義 'meaningful'. The meaning of a word or what someone means is 意思 yì si.

example.pinyin: Zhè jiàn shì duì wǒ hěn yǒu yìyì.
example.english: This means a lot to me.

note: Come in toward where the speaker is; 進去 jìn qù means 'go in'. After another verb it means 'in (toward here)': 走進來 'walk in'.

example.pinyin: Mén méi suǒ, qǐng jìnlái ba.
example.english: The door's unlocked, come on in.

note: Also a noun: one's experiences or background. For know-how or skill gained, 經驗 jīng yàn is used.

example.english: She has been through a lot.

note: 行 is read háng here (a business or trade). As 'to walk / OK' it is xíng.

example.pinyin: Wǒ yào qù yínháng lǐng qián.
example.english: I need to go to the bank to take out money.

note: Counted with 把 bǎ: 一把鑰匙 yī bǎ yào shi 'a key'. MOE reads the second syllable light (yào shi).
Means going in, away from where the speaker is; 進來 jìn lái is 'come in'. Also follows other verbs: 走進去 zǒu jìn qù 'walk in'. Often pronounced lightly as jìn qu.

In Taiwan, 讀書 dú shū and 讀大學 mean 'to study / attend school'; 念 niàn (念書, 念大學) is an equally common synonym. For reading a book silently, people usually say 看書 kàn shū. The rare reading dòu means a pause in a sentence.

example.english: He goes to university in Taipei.

note: Works for doors, boxes, bottles, and switching on devices (打開電視 dǎ kāi diàn shì). Plain 開 kāi is also used for the same things.

hint: a time word, not gāng gāng
note: A time word for 'a moment ago'. Taiwanese more often say 剛剛 gāng gāng, which means the same thing.
A bit more formal or general than plain 學 xué. In casual speech people say 學中文 xué zhōng wén more than 學習中文. MOE also lists xué xi, but Taiwan speech uses xué xí.

hint: formal money unit, spoken is kuài
note: The formal unit of money (in Taiwan, NT dollars). You see and hear it on prices and announcements: 一百元 yī bǎi yuán. In everyday talk Taiwanese say 塊 kuài.

example.english: A cup of coffee is eighty dollars.

note: In Taiwan this is the motor scooter, the most common way to get around: 騎機車 qí jī chē 'ride a scooter'. As slang, 很機車 hěn jī chē describes an annoying, difficult person. On the mainland 機車 means a locomotive.

example.english: I ride my scooter to work.

note: Cooked rice is 飯 fàn. On the mainland 米 also means 'meter'; Taiwan usually says 公尺 gōng chǐ.

example.english: We're out of rice at home.

note: Literally 'see again'. Casually, Taiwanese often say 掰掰 bāi bāi.
Also a noun for sports or exercise, and for a social or political movement. MOE also lists yùn dong, but Taiwan speech normally uses yùn dòng.

hint: lay out the details, e.g. instructions
note: Explaining how or what something is. 解釋 jiě shì leans more toward explaining why. 說明書 shuō míng shū is an instruction manual.

example.english: Let me explain it to you.

note: 洗手 xǐ shǒu 'wash your hands', 洗碗 xǐ wǎn 'do the dishes', 洗衣服 xǐ yī fu 'do the laundry', 洗頭 xǐ tóu 'wash your hair'. 洗澡 xǐ zǎo is 'to shower'.
Goes at the end of a noun phrase: 我最好的朋友之一 'one of my best friends'.

example.trad: 這是我最喜歡的歌之一。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì wǒ zuì xǐhuān de gē zhīyī.
example.english: This is one of my favorite songs.
